newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Arafat receives rousing welcome in Nablus.
newsitem.headline: Arafat receives rousing welcome in Nablus.

text.p: Palestinians in the Israeli-blockaded West Bank town of Nablus gave a rousing welcome on Saturday to Palestinian President Yasser Arafat.

"We sacrifice our blood and soul for you Abu Ammar," thousands chanted using Arafat's nom de guerre as his helicopter set down in the town still ringed by Israeli tanks deployed during Israeli-Palestinian clashes last month.
Arafat was to chair a joint meeting of the Palestinian Authority's cabinet and the Palestine Liberation Organisation executive.
U.S. Middle East peace envoy Dennis Ross would join Arafat in Nablus for lunch later in the day, Arafat's adviser Nabil Abu Rdainah told Reuters.
Ross is mediating in negotiations that began this week between Israel and the Palestinians on implementing a long-delayed Israeli troop redeployment in the West Bank town of Hebron.

The Hebron redeployment should have been carried out in March but was delayed by the previous Israeli government in the wake of Islamic militant suicide bombings that killed 59 people in Israel in March and February.

It was frozen by Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu who is demanding changes in the signed deal which he says are necessary to ensure the security of some 400 Jewish settlers who live in heavily armed enclaves in the heart of the town amidst 100,000 Palestinians.
Palestinians insist the signed deal cannot be changed.
Despite the differences in the talks -- which Arafat said on Thursday had shown no progress -- Palestinians on Friday gave mixed assessments on the prospects for a breakthrough.

Negotiator Hassan Asfour said there had been no progress but West Bank security chief Jibril Rajoub said he was "100 percent" certain Israel and the PLO would soon agree on the long-delayed Israeli redeployment in Hebron.
Arafat plans to visit Jordan next week for talks on Middle East peace efforts.
Jordan's King Hussein has become outspokenly critical of Netanyahu since controversy erupted over Israel's opening of a new entrance to a tourist tunnel near Moslem holy sites in Arab East Jerusalem.
The tunnel controversy sparked violence last month in which 60 Arabs and 15 Israeli soldiers died.
Waqf (Islamic Trust) officials opened the al-Aqsa mosque complex, Islam's third holiest site, to tourists on Saturday for the first time since the fighting.
